content: In rapidly evolving and high-risk situations, local treatment guidelines for malaria cannot always rely on robust evidence. However, the potential risks of continuing ineffective treatment regimens are likely to outweigh the risks associated with introducing new, untested regimens, especially when using antimalarial drugs with established safety profiles. For example, combinations such as artesunate and pyronaridine may prove effective. There is an urgent need for studies to identify optimal treatments for artemisinin-resistant malaria. The quality of antimalarial drugs is a critical concern. Poor-quality medicines fall into two categories: falsified drugs, which are intentionally counterfeit and often contain little or no active pharmaceutical ingredients (and sometimes harmful substances), and substandard drugs, which are produced by legitimate manufacturers but fail to meet quality standards due to incorrect amounts of active ingredients, improper formulation, or degradation from poor storage conditions. Falsified antimalarial drugs, including tablets and ampoules with insufficient active ingredients, are a significant issue in some regions. These counterfeit drugs are often indistinguishable from genuine products at the point of care, leading to under-dosing, high treatment failure rates, and the mistaken impression of drug resistance. They may also contribute to the development of resistance by maintaining sub-therapeutic blood levels or contain toxic substances. Substandard drugs arise from poor manufacturing practices, chemical instability, or improper storage. Artemisinin and its derivatives are particularly prone to chemical instability, which is essential for their biological activity but creates challenges in manufacturing and co-formulation with other compounds. These stability issues are exacerbated in tropical climates. Therefore, stringent quality standards are especially important for this class of drugs. Many antimalarial drugs are stored in conditions of high heat and humidity and are often sold beyond their expiration dates. In malaria-endemic areas, a significant proportion of antimalarial drugs are generic products purchased in the private sector. While these may contain the correct amounts of active ingredients, their formulation may result in inadequate absorption. Antimalarial medicines must be manufactured according to good manufacturing practices, contain the correct drug and excipient contents, demonstrate bioavailability comparable to reference products, be stored under appropriate conditions, and be dispensed before their expiration dates. Tools to assess drug quality at points of sale are under development, but the capacity of regulatory agencies in many countries to monitor drug quality remains limited. Strengthening legal and regulatory frameworks and fostering collaboration between law enforcement, customs, and regulatory agencies are essential to combat falsified medicines effectively. Private-sector drug distribution outlets should be better informed and actively engaged with regulatory agencies. The World Health Organization (WHO), in collaboration with other United Nations agencies, has established an international mechanism to prequalify manufacturers of artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) based on their compliance with internationally recommended manufacturing and quality standards. Countries should strengthen their systems for monitoring and evaluating national malaria programs when adapting and implementing these guidelines. These systems should enable countries to track the implementation and impact of new recommendations, better target programs to areas and populations in greatest need, and detect decreasing antimalarial efficacy and drug resistance as early as possible. Routine surveillance is essential for universal diagnostic testing, antimalarial treatment, and strengthened malaria surveillance systems. The test, track, treat initiative recommends testing every suspected malaria case, treating every confirmed case with quality-assured antimalarial medicine, and tracking the disease through timely and accurate surveillance systems. Surveillance and treatment based on confirmed malaria cases will improve understanding of the disease burden and enable national malaria control programs to allocate resources more effectively. Therapeutic efficacy monitoring for falciparum malaria involves assessing clinical and parasitological outcomes of treatment for at least 28 days after initiating adequate treatment and monitoring for the reappearance of parasites in the blood. The duration of post-treatment follow-up depends on the elimination half-life of the partner drug in the ACT being evaluated. Tools for monitoring antimalarial drug efficacy are available on the WHO website. PCR genotyping should be used in therapeutic monitoring to distinguish between recrudescence (true treatment failure) and new infections. Monitoring should also include confirmation of drug quality, molecular genotyping to identify genetic markers of drug resistance, studies of parasite susceptibility in culture, and measurement of antimalarial drug levels in cases of slow therapeutic response or treatment failure. Governments should establish effective pharmacovigilance systems to monitor the safety of all drugs, including antimalarial medicines. While the safety profiles of currently recommended antimalarial drugs are reasonably well-documented, rare but serious adverse drug reactions may not be detected in clinical trials due to their limited size and underrepresentation of vulnerable populations such as young children, pregnant women, or individuals with concurrent illnesses. These rare adverse reactions are typically identified only in prospective phase IV post-marketing studies or population-based pharmacovigilance systems. More data are urgently needed on the safety of ACTs during the first trimester of pregnancy and on potential interactions between antimalarial and other commonly used medicines. Routine monitoring of antimalarial drug efficacy is necessary to ensure effective case management and early detection of resistance. WHO recommends testing the efficacy of firstand second-line antimalarial treatments at least once every 24 months at all sentinel sites. Data collected from studies conducted according to standard protocols inform national treatment policies. Tools and materials for conducting routine therapeutic efficacy studies (TES) are available and serve as references for national programs and investigators conducting routine surveillance studies to assess the efficacy of registered medicines. National malaria programs should regularly monitor the therapeutic efficacy of antimalarial drugs using standard WHO protocols. These guidelines provide a generic framework for malaria diagnosis and treatment policies worldwide. However, national policymakers must adapt these recommendations based on local priorities, malaria epidemiology, parasite resistance, and national resources. Decision-making should involve inclusive, transparent, and rigorous approaches, engaging a broad range of stakeholders to ensure feasibility, appropriateness, equity, and acceptability. Transparency and freedom from financial conflicts of interest will reduce mistrust and conflict, while evidence-based processes will ensure the best possible decisions for the population. Reliable national data on the efficacy of antimalarial medicines and parasite resistance are essential for selecting firstand second-line treatments. This requires appropriate surveillance and monitoring systems. In some countries, the group adapting the guidelines for national use may need to re-evaluate the global evidence base in their local context. The GRADE tables may serve as a starting point for this assessment. Decisions about coverage, feasibility, acceptability, and cost may require input from various health professionals, community representatives, health economists, academics, and health system managers. Failure to implement the principles of combination therapy and rational use of antimalarial medicines risks promoting the emergence and spread of drug resistance, potentially undoing recent gains in malaria control and elimination. The recommendations in these guidelines provide an opportunity to improve malaria case management, reduce unnecessary morbidity and mortality, and contribute to ongoing elimination efforts.
